notes.front: What is the Hazardous Materials Table (HMT)?
notes.explanation: For each listed material it gives the hazard class (or says the material is forbidden) and the proper shipping name.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(a), p. 3
notes.evidence: The Hazardous Materials Table (Table) in this section designates the materials listed therein as hazardous materials for the purpose of transportation of those materials.
notes.back: The table in § 172.101 that designates the materials listed in it as hazardous materials for transportation.
notes.example: Like an index at the back of the regulations: look up the material and it points you to its class, name and further rules.

notes.front: What does “n.o.s.” mean in a shipping description?
notes.explanation: An n.o.s. description is a shipping description from the § 172.101 table that includes the abbreviation n.o.s.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 171 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 171.8, “N.O.S.”, p. 32
notes.evidence: N.O.S. means not otherwise specified. N.O.S. description means a shipping description from the § 172.101 table which includes the abbreviation n.o.s.
notes.back: Not otherwise specified.
notes.example: Like a catch-all drawer marked “other”: used for a material the table does not name.

notes.front: What does column 4 of the HMT give for each proper shipping name?
notes.explanation: Each proper shipping name in the table has an identification number assigned to it in column 4.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(e), p. 7
notes.evidence: Column 4 lists the identification number assigned to each proper shipping name.
notes.back: Its identification number (ID number).
notes.example: Like a catalogue number that goes with each product name.

notes.front: What does the prefix “UN” on an identification number show?
notes.explanation: The prefix tells you where the name is recognised, not how dangerous the material is.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(e), p. 7
notes.evidence: Those preceded by the letters ‘‘UN’’ are associated with proper shipping names considered appropriate for international transportation as well as domestic transportation.
notes.back: The proper shipping name is considered appropriate for international as well as domestic transportation.
notes.example: Like a passport stamp: the name is good both at home and abroad.

notes.front: What does the prefix “NA” on an identification number show?
notes.explanation: An NA number is for a name used only in the United States.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(e), p. 7
notes.evidence: Those preceded by the letters ‘‘NA’’ are associated with proper shipping names not recognized for transportation outside of the United States.
notes.back: The proper shipping name is not recognised for transportation outside the United States.
notes.example: Like a local ticket that is valid only within one country.

notes.front: What is a special provision, as referred to in column 7 of the HMT?
notes.explanation: Special provisions cover packaging provisions, prohibitions, exceptions and mode-specific rules.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(h), p. 8
notes.evidence: When Column 7 refers to a special provision for a hazardous material, the meaning and requirements of that special provision are as set forth in § 172.102 of this subpart.
notes.back: A coded requirement for a hazardous material whose meaning and requirements are set out in § 172.102.
notes.example: Like a footnote number in a table: the code sends you to the text that applies.

notes.front: What is a marine pollutant?
notes.explanation: The listing and the concentration thresholds together define the term.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 171 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 171.8, “Marine pollutant”, p. 30
notes.evidence: Marine pollutant, means a material which is listed in appendix B to § 172.101 of this subchapter (also see § 171.4) and, when in a solution or mixture of one or more marine pollutants, is packaged in a concentration which equals or exceeds:
notes.back: A material listed in appendix B to § 172.101 that, in a solution or mixture, is at or above a set concentration.
notes.example: Like a listed chemical that counts only once its share of the mixture reaches the threshold.

notes.front: For each listed material, what two things does the HMT identify?
notes.explanation: Where a name is not the preferred one, the table directs the user to the preferred proper shipping name.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(a), p. 3
notes.evidence: For each listed material, the Table identifies the hazard class or specifies that the material is forbidden in transportation, and gives the proper shipping name or directs the user to the preferred proper shipping name.
notes.back: The hazard class (or that the material is forbidden), and the proper shipping name (or the preferred one).

notes.front: What are two further kinds of requirement the HMT specifies or references?
notes.explanation: The table points to these requirements elsewhere in the regulations.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(a), p. 3
notes.evidence: the Table specifies or references requirements in this subchapter pertaining to labeling, packaging, quantity limits aboard aircraft and stowage of hazardous materials aboard vessels.
notes.back: Any two of: labelling, packaging, quantity limits aboard aircraft, stowage aboard vessels.

notes.front: A material is not named in the HMT. Tests show it is not a forbidden material and meets the definition of no hazard class. What is it for transportation purposes?
notes.explanation: Section 172.101(c)(12)(iv) says such a material is not a hazardous material.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(c)(12)(iv), p. 6
notes.evidence: If it is specifically determined that a material is not a forbidden material and does not meet the definition of any hazard class, the material is not a hazardous material.
notes.back: C: Not a hazardous material
notes.choices:
A) A Class 9 material, by default
B) An n.o.s. material in the class it comes closest to
C) Not a hazardous material
D) A forbidden material until it is listed
notes.choicesExplained: A: Class 9 still needs a material that presents a hazard in transportation. B: an n.o.s. description is chosen only for a material that meets a hazard class definition. D: the tests showed it is not a forbidden material.

notes.front: Column 1 of the HMT contains {{c1::six}} symbols: +, A, D, G, I and W.
notes.explanation: Each symbol changes how an entry's name or requirements apply.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(b), p. 3
notes.evidence: Column 1 of the Table contains six symbols (‘‘ + ’’, ‘‘A’’, ‘‘D’’, ‘‘G’’, ‘‘I’’ and ‘‘W’’) as follows:

notes.front: What does a plus sign (+) in column 1 fix for an entry?
notes.explanation: A plus sign also means the material is known to pose a risk to humans.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(b)(1), p. 3
notes.evidence: The plus (+) sign fixes the proper shipping name, hazard class and packing group for that entry without regard to whether the material meets the definition of that class, packing group or any other hazard class definition.
notes.back: The proper shipping name, hazard class and packing group, whether or not the material meets that class's definition.

notes.front: An HMT entry for a named material carries a plus sign in column 1. A shipper's own tests suggest the material would fall in a lower packing group. What applies?
notes.explanation: The plus sign fixes the entry's name, class and packing group without regard to whether the material meets the definitions.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(b)(1), p. 3
notes.evidence: The plus (+) sign fixes the proper shipping name, hazard class and packing group for that entry without regard to whether the material meets the definition of that class, packing group or any other hazard class definition.
notes.back: D: The name, class and packing group shown for the entry
notes.choices:
A) Whichever the shipper prefers, if marked on the package
B) The packing group the shipper's tests support
C) An n.o.s. description chosen from the tests
D) The name, class and packing group shown for the entry
notes.choicesExplained: B: the plus sign fixes the packing group regardless of the definitions. C: the rule for choosing another name applies except when the name is preceded by a plus. A: the plus sign leaves no choice.

notes.front: What does the letter A in column 1 mean?
notes.explanation: An A entry may still be used to describe the material for other modes if all its requirements are met.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(b)(2), p. 3
notes.evidence: The letter ‘‘A’’ denotes a material that is subject to the requirements of this subchapter only when offered or intended for transportation by aircraft, unless the material is a hazardous substance or a hazardous waste.
notes.back: The material is subject to the regulations only when offered or intended for transport by aircraft, unless it is a hazardous substance or hazardous waste.

notes.front: What does the letter W in column 1 mean?
notes.explanation: A W entry may still be used to describe the material for other modes if all its requirements are met.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(b)(6), p. 3
notes.evidence: The letter ‘‘W’’ denotes a material that is subject to the requirements of this subchapter only when offered or intended for transportation by vessel, unless the material is a hazardous substance or a hazardous waste.
notes.back: The material is subject to the regulations only when offered or intended for transport by vessel, unless it is a hazardous substance or hazardous waste.

notes.front: What does the letter D in column 1 identify?
notes.explanation: A D name may not suit international rules, and the table lets an alternate proper shipping name be chosen whether transport is domestic or international.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(b)(3), p. 3
notes.evidence: The letter ‘‘D’’ identifies proper shipping names which are appropriate for describing materials for domestic transportation but may be inappropriate for international transportation
notes.back: Proper shipping names appropriate for domestic transportation but possibly inappropriate for international transportation.

notes.front: What does the letter I in column 1 identify?
notes.explanation: An alternate proper shipping name may be selected when only domestic transportation is involved.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(b)(5), p. 3
notes.evidence: The letter ‘‘I’’ identifies proper shipping names which are appropriate for describing materials in international transportation. An alternate proper shipping name may be selected when only domestic transportation is involved.
notes.back: Proper shipping names appropriate for describing materials in international transportation.

notes.front: What does the letter G in column 1 require?
notes.explanation: G entries are generic names, so the technical name tells what the material actually is.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(b)(4), p. 3
notes.evidence: The letter ‘‘G’’ identifies proper shipping names for which one or more technical names of the hazardous material must be entered in parentheses, in association with the basic description.
notes.back: One or more technical names of the hazardous material entered in parentheses with the basic description.

notes.front: An HMT entry carries the letter A in column 1. The material is neither a hazardous substance nor a hazardous waste, and it will travel only by highway. Is it subject to the regulations?
notes.explanation: The A symbol limits the regulations to air transport, with the hazardous substance and waste exceptions.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(b)(2), p. 3
notes.evidence: The letter ‘‘A’’ denotes a material that is subject to the requirements of this subchapter only when offered or intended for transportation by aircraft, unless the material is a hazardous substance or a hazardous waste.
notes.back: B: No: an A material is subject only when offered or intended for transport by aircraft
notes.choices:
A) Yes: every material in the table is regulated in every mode
B) No: an A material is subject only when offered or intended for transport by aircraft
C) Only if it is carried by vessel
D) Yes, but only its packaging rules apply
notes.choicesExplained: A: the A and W symbols limit an entry to air or to vessel transport. D: the A symbol makes the material not subject at all outside air transport, unless it is a hazardous substance or waste. C: vessel-only entries carry the letter W, not A.

notes.front: Proper shipping names in column 2 are limited to those shown in {{c1::Roman type (not italics)}}.
notes.explanation: Words in italics and punctuation are not part of the proper shipping name, though they may be used in addition to it.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(c), p. 3
notes.evidence: Proper shipping names are limited to those shown in Roman type (not italics).

notes.front: A column 2 entry shows a name in Roman type followed by a phrase in italics. Which part is the proper shipping name?
notes.explanation: Italic words may be used in addition to the proper shipping name but are not part of it.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(c)(2), p. 4
notes.evidence: Punctuation marks and words in italics are not part of the proper shipping name, but may be used in addition to the proper shipping name.
notes.back: A: The part in Roman type; the italic phrase may be added but is not part of the name
notes.choices:
A) The part in Roman type; the italic phrase may be added but is not part of the name
B) The italic phrase, because it is more specific
C) The whole line, italics included
D) Either part, as the shipper chooses
notes.choicesExplained: C: words in italics are not part of the proper shipping name. B: proper shipping names are limited to Roman type. D: only the Roman type is the proper shipping name.

notes.front: May the word “inflammable” be used in place of “flammable” in a proper shipping name?
notes.explanation: Other alternative spellings, such as “aluminium” for “aluminum” and “sulphur” for “sulfur”, are allowed.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(c)(1), p. 3
notes.evidence: ‘‘sulfur’’ may be spelled ‘‘sulphur’’. However, the word ‘‘inflammable’’ may not
notes.back: No.

notes.front: When may “poison” or “poisonous” be used interchangeably with “toxic” in a proper shipping name?
notes.explanation: The same paragraph lets “n.o.i.” or “n.o.i.b.n.” be used interchangeably with “n.o.s.”.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(c)(3), p. 4
notes.evidence: The word ‘‘poison’’ or ‘‘poisonous’’ may be used interchangeably with the word ‘‘toxic’’ when only domestic transportation is involved.
notes.back: Only when domestic transportation alone is involved.

notes.front: The column 2 description of a material does not include the word “waste”. How must its proper shipping name read when it is shipped as a hazardous waste?
notes.explanation: The waste prefix is added only where the table description does not already contain the word.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(c)(9), p. 4
notes.evidence: If the word ‘‘waste’’ is not included in the hazardous material description in Column 2 of the Table, the proper shipping name for a hazardous waste (as defined in § 171.8 of this subchapter), shall include the word ‘‘Waste’’ preceding the proper shipping name of the material.
notes.back: With the word “Waste” before the proper shipping name.

notes.front: A plant ships a spent solvent as a hazardous waste. Its HMT entry name does not contain the word “waste”. What must the shipper do with the name?
notes.explanation: A hazardous waste takes the prefix “Waste” when the table description lacks it.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(c)(9), p. 4
notes.evidence: the proper shipping name for a hazardous waste (as defined in § 171.8 of this subchapter), shall include the word ‘‘Waste’’ preceding the proper shipping name of the material.
notes.back: D: Put the word “Waste” before the proper shipping name
notes.choices:
A) Nothing; waste status appears only on the manifest
B) Add “waste” after the name, in italics
C) Use an n.o.s. description instead
D) Put the word “Waste” before the proper shipping name
notes.choicesExplained: B: the word “Waste” must precede the proper shipping name. C: the named entry still applies; only the prefix is added. A: the proper shipping name for a hazardous waste must include the word “Waste”.

notes.front: A mixture not named in the table is made of one predominant hazardous material, which the table names by technical name, plus other materials. How is it usually described?
notes.explanation: The rule has exceptions, such as when the mixture's hazard class or packing group differs from the entry's.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(c)(10)(i), p. 4
notes.evidence: must be described using the proper shipping name of the hazardous material and the qualifying word ‘‘mixture’’ or ‘‘solution’’, as appropriate, unless—
notes.back: By that material's proper shipping name plus the word “mixture” or “solution”, as appropriate.

notes.front: If no appropriate technical name is shown in the table, where is the proper shipping name chosen from?
notes.explanation: The name that most appropriately describes the material is to be used.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(c)(12)(ii), p. 5
notes.evidence: If an appropriate technical name is not shown in the Table, selection of a proper shipping name shall be made from the generic or n.o.s. descriptions corresponding to the specific hazard class, packing group, hazard zone, or subsidiary hazard, if any, for the material.
notes.back: The generic or n.o.s. descriptions matching the material's hazard class, packing group, hazard zone and any subsidiary hazard.

notes.front: A corrosive liquid is not named in the HMT, so the shipper picks a generic n.o.s. entry that carries G in column 1. What must go with the basic description?
notes.explanation: The n.o.s. rule chooses the generic entry, and the G symbol then calls for the technical name.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(b)(4), p. 3
notes.evidence: The letter ‘‘G’’ identifies proper shipping names for which one or more technical names of the hazardous material must be entered in parentheses, in association with the basic description.
notes.back: A: The technical name of the hazardous material, in parentheses
notes.choices:
A) The technical name of the hazardous material, in parentheses
B) The word “Waste” in front of the name
C) The phrase “not otherwise specified” in full
D) Nothing: n.o.s. entries need no further detail
notes.choicesExplained: D: a G entry requires the technical name in parentheses. B: that prefix is for hazardous wastes. C: the abbreviation n.o.s. is part of the name; the G symbol asks for the technical name.

notes.front: What may a sample whose hazard class is uncertain and must be found by testing be given before it is shipped?
notes.explanation: The determination uses the defining criteria, the § 173.2a hazard precedence and the shipper's knowledge of the material.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(c)(11), p. 5
notes.evidence: a sample of a material for which the hazard class is uncertain and must be determined by testing may be assigned a tentative proper shipping name, hazard class, identification number and packing group, if applicable, based on the shipper’s tentative determination
notes.back: A tentative proper shipping name, hazard class, ID number and packing group, based on the shipper's tentative determination.

notes.front: When does a Class 3 reference in column 3 read “Combustible liquid” instead?
notes.explanation: Column 3 otherwise shows the hazard class or division, or the word “Forbidden”.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(d)(4), p. 7
notes.evidence: Each reference to a Class 3 material is modified to read ‘‘Combustible liquid’’ when that material is reclassified in accordance with § 173.150(e) or (f) of this subchapter or has a flash point above 60 °C (140 °F) but below 93 °C (200 °F).
notes.back: When the material is reclassified under § 173.150(e) or (f), or has a flash point above 60 °C but below 93 °C.

notes.front: Column 3 of an entry shows Class 3. The shipper's material under that entry has a flash point of 70 °C. How is the column 3 reference read for this material?
notes.explanation: A flash point of 70 °C is above 60 °C and below 93 °C.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(d)(4), p. 7
notes.evidence: has a flash point above 60 °C (140 °F) but below 93 °C (200 °F).
notes.back: B: As “Combustible liquid”
notes.choices:
A) As Class 3, unchanged
B) As “Combustible liquid”
C) As “Forbidden”
D) As Class 9
notes.choicesExplained: A: the reference is modified to read “Combustible liquid” for a flash point above 60 °C and below 93 °C. C: nothing in the case makes the material forbidden. D: column 3 is modified to “Combustible liquid”, not to Class 9.

notes.front: What does the prefix “ID” on an identification number show?
notes.explanation: Column 4 uses three prefixes: UN, NA and ID.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(e), p. 7
notes.evidence: Those preceded by the letters ‘‘ID’’ are associated with proper shipping names recognized by the ICAO Technical Instructions
notes.back: The proper shipping name is recognised by the International Civil Aviation Organization's Technical Instructions.

notes.front: A shipper plans to send a material described under an NA-numbered proper shipping name on an international voyage. What does the NA prefix tell the shipper?
notes.explanation: NA numbers go with proper shipping names that are not recognised outside the United States.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(e), p. 7
notes.evidence: Those preceded by the letters ‘‘NA’’ are associated with proper shipping names not recognized for transportation outside of the United States.
notes.back: B: That proper shipping name is not recognised for transport outside the United States
notes.choices:
A) The name is valid worldwide
B) That proper shipping name is not recognised for transport outside the United States
C) The name is recognised only for air transport
D) The material is forbidden in every mode
notes.choicesExplained: A: that is what a UN prefix shows. C: air recognition is shown by the ID prefix. D: the prefix concerns where the name is recognised, not whether the material is forbidden.

notes.front: Which identification numbers may a Category A infectious substance be assigned?
notes.explanation: The choice rests on the medical history or symptoms of the source, endemic local conditions, or professional judgement.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.134(a)(1)(i), p. 120
notes.evidence: A Category A infectious substance must be assigned to identification number UN2814, UN2900, or UN3549, as appropriate.
notes.back: UN 2814, UN 2900 or UN 3549, as appropriate.

notes.front: A Category B infectious substance is assigned identification number {{c1::UN 3373}}.
notes.explanation: Regulated medical waste is not included; it takes UN 3291.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 173.134(a)(1)(ii), p. 121
notes.evidence: A Category B infectious substance must be described as ‘‘Biological substance, Category B’’ and assigned identification number UN3373. This does not include regulated medical waste, which must be assigned identification number UN3291.

notes.front: In column 6, what do the first label code and any further label codes indicate?
notes.explanation: Column 6 codes stand for the hazard warning labels required on a package of the material.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(g), p. 7
notes.evidence: The first code is indicative of the primary hazard of the material. Additional label codes are indicative of subsidiary hazards.
notes.back: The first code indicates the primary hazard; additional codes indicate subsidiary hazards.

notes.front: Is a label required for a combustible liquid, or for a Class 3 material reclassed as a combustible liquid?
notes.explanation: Column 6 states this exception directly.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(g), p. 7
notes.evidence: No label is required for a material classed as a combustible liquid or for a Class 3 material that is reclassed as a combustible liquid.
notes.back: No.

notes.front: Column 6 of an entry lists the label codes 3 and 8, in that order. What do they tell you?
notes.explanation: The first code shows the primary hazard; later codes show subsidiary hazards.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(g), p. 7
notes.evidence: The first code is indicative of the primary hazard of the material. Additional label codes are indicative of subsidiary hazards.
notes.back: C: Class 3 is the primary hazard and Class 8 a subsidiary hazard
notes.choices:
A) Class 8 is the primary hazard because it is listed last
B) The shipper may choose either label
C) Class 3 is the primary hazard and Class 8 a subsidiary hazard
D) Both are primary hazards of equal rank
notes.choicesExplained: A: the first code is the primary hazard. B: the codes stand for the labels required on the package. D: additional codes indicate subsidiary hazards.

notes.front: What does a special provision code made only of numbers mean?
notes.explanation: Codes with letters are limited to a mode or a type of packaging.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.102(b)(1), p. 200
notes.evidence: A code consisting only of numbers (for example, ‘‘11’’) is multi-modal in application and may apply to bulk and non-bulk packagings.
notes.back: It is multi-modal and may apply to bulk and non-bulk packagings.

notes.front: To what does a special provision code containing the letter B apply?
notes.explanation: Unless otherwise provided, B codes do not apply to portable tanks or intermediate bulk containers.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.102(b)(3), p. 200
notes.evidence: A code containing the letter ‘‘B’’ refers to a special provision that applies only to bulk packaging requirements.
notes.back: Only to bulk packaging requirements.

notes.front: Column 7 of an entry lists a code containing the letter T. The shipper is filling non-bulk drums for a road journey. Does that code apply to this shipment?
notes.explanation: A T code refers to a special provision that applies only to portable tanks.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.102(b)(7), p. 200
notes.evidence: A code containing the letter ‘‘T’’ refers to a special provision which applies only to transportation in UN or IM Specification portable tanks.
notes.back: C: No: T codes apply only to transport in certain specification portable tanks
notes.choices:
A) Yes: every column 7 code applies to every shipment
B) Yes, because it is a road journey
C) No: T codes apply only to transport in certain specification portable tanks
D) Only if the drums hold more than 450 L
notes.choicesExplained: A: codes containing letters are limited to a mode or a type of packaging. B: T codes are about portable tanks, not about the highway mode. D: the T code applies to portable tanks, whatever the drum size.

notes.front: What does column 8A of the HMT specify?
notes.explanation: Columns 8A, 8B and 8C are read with “§ 173.” in front of the number shown.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(i), p. 8
notes.evidence: Columns 8A, 8B and 8C specify the applicable sections for exceptions, nonbulk packaging requirements and bulk packaging requirements, respectively, in part 173 of this subchapter.
notes.back: The part 173 section giving exceptions for the material.

notes.front: What does column 8B of the HMT specify?
notes.explanation: A “None” in column 8B means non-bulk packagings are not authorized, except as special provisions in column 7 allow.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(i)(2), p. 8
notes.evidence: Column 8B references the section in part 173 of this subchapter which prescribes packaging requirements for non-bulk packagings.
notes.back: The part 173 section giving the non-bulk packaging requirements.

notes.front: What does column 8C of the HMT specify?
notes.explanation: A “None” in column 8C means bulk packagings are not authorized, except as columns 7 and 8B provide.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(i)(3), p. 8
notes.evidence: Column (8C) specifies the section in part 173 of this subchapter that prescribes packaging requirements for bulk packagings
notes.back: The part 173 section giving the bulk packaging requirements.

notes.front: For a liquid, column 8B shows “203” and column 8C shows “241”. The shipper will use a bulk packaging. Which section sets the packaging requirements?
notes.explanation: Column 8C gives the bulk packaging section, read with “§ 173.” in front.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(i), p. 8
notes.evidence: Columns 8A, 8B and 8C are completed in a manner which indicates that ‘‘§ 173.’’ precedes the designated numerical entry.
notes.choicesExplained: A: column 8B is for non-bulk packagings. C: column 8 entries are read with “§ 173.” in front. D: § 173.24 applies to all packagings in addition to the column 8 section.

notes.front: What does column 9A of the HMT limit?
notes.explanation: The limit is net unless otherwise specified.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(j), p. 9
notes.evidence: Columns 9A and 9B specify the maximum quantities that may be offered for transportation in one package by passenger-carrying aircraft or passengercarrying rail car (Column 9A) or by cargo aircraft only (Column 9B)
notes.back: The maximum quantity in one package by passenger-carrying aircraft or passenger-carrying rail car.

notes.front: What does column 9B of the HMT limit?
notes.explanation: “Forbidden” in column 9 means the material may not be offered or transported in that mode.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(j), p. 9
notes.evidence: or by cargo aircraft only (Column 9B), subject to the following: (1) ‘‘Forbidden’’ means the material may not be offered for transportation or transported in the applicable mode of transport.
notes.back: The maximum quantity in one package by cargo aircraft only.

notes.front: An entry shows “Forbidden” in column 9A and “25 kg” in column 9B. How may the material travel by air?
notes.explanation: Column 9A covers passenger aircraft and passenger rail cars; column 9B covers cargo aircraft only.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(j), p. 9
notes.evidence: (1) ‘‘Forbidden’’ means the material may not be offered for transportation or transported in the applicable mode of transport.
notes.back: A: By cargo aircraft only, up to 25 kg per package
notes.choices:
A) By cargo aircraft only, up to 25 kg per package
B) Not by air at all
C) By passenger aircraft, up to 25 kg per package
D) By passenger rail car, up to 25 kg
notes.choicesExplained: C: “Forbidden” in 9A rules out passenger-carrying aircraft. B: column 9B allows cargo aircraft up to its limit. D: column 9A also covers passenger-carrying rail cars, and it reads “Forbidden”.

notes.front: What do columns 10A and 10B of the HMT specify?
notes.explanation: Limited quantities are allocated stowage category A and are not subject to the 10B codes.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 172.101(k), p. 9
notes.evidence: Column 10A [Vessel stowage] specifies the authorized stowage locations on board cargo and passenger ves- sels. Column 10B [Other provisions] specifies codes for stowage and handling requirements for specific hazardous materials.
notes.back: 10A: authorized stowage locations on cargo and passenger vessels; 10B: codes for stowage and handling requirements.

notes.front: What does appendix A to § 172.101 list (in the 1 October 2025 text)?
notes.explanation: It is split into two tables: substances other than radionuclides, and radionuclides.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), Appendix A to § 172.101, p. 169
notes.evidence: This appendix lists materials and their corresponding reportable quantities (RQ’s) that are listed or designated as ‘‘hazardous substances’’ under section 101(14) of the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act
notes.back: Hazardous substances and their reportable quantities, as designated under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act.

notes.front: From what date does appendix A to § 172.101 stop listing hazardous substances and refer to the Environmental Protection Agency's list instead?
notes.explanation: Until that date, appendix A itself lists the substances and their reportable quantities.
notes.source: Hazardous Materials: Remove Redundant List of U.S. EPA CERCLA Hazardous Substances, 91 FR 49305 (4 August 2026), Dates, p. 1
notes.evidence: DATES: This final rule is effective December 2, 2026.
notes.back: 2 December 2026, when the final rule published in August 2026 takes effect.

notes.front: From 2 December 2026, where does appendix A to § 172.101 send the reader for hazardous substances and reportable quantities?
notes.explanation: The appendix keeps its title but its list is replaced by this reference.
notes.source: Hazardous Materials: Remove Redundant List of U.S. EPA CERCLA Hazardous Substances, 91 FR 49305 (4 August 2026), Amendment to appendix A to § 172.101, p. 6
notes.evidence: Refer to 40 CFR 302.4 to see the list of hazardous substances and their reportable quantities (RQs) in Table 302.4. The list includes an Appendix B to § 302.4 for radionuclides and their adjusted RQs.
notes.back: To Table 302.4 in title 40, section 302.4 (with its Appendix B for radionuclides).

notes.front: Does the 2026 change to appendix A alter whether a material is classified as a hazardous substance?
notes.explanation: The final rule states that it does not functionally change the classification.
notes.source: Hazardous Materials: Remove Redundant List of U.S. EPA CERCLA Hazardous Substances, 91 FR 49305 (4 August 2026), Section I.B, p. 2
notes.evidence: because this action simply modifies how the list is referenced within the Code of Federal Regulations, it does not functionally change whether a material is classified as a hazardous substance.
notes.back: No. It changes only how the list is referenced.

notes.front: In January 2027 a shipper needs the reportable quantity of a hazardous substance. Where should the shipper look?
notes.explanation: After 2 December 2026, persons offering such materials must refer to the title 40 list for substances and their reportable quantities.
notes.source: Hazardous Materials: Remove Redundant List of U.S. EPA CERCLA Hazardous Substances, 91 FR 49305 (4 August 2026), Section I.B, p. 2
notes.evidence: persons offering for transportation and transporting materials that may be subject to hazardous substance requirements in the HMR must refer to the EPA regulations at 40 CFR 302.4 for the list of regulated hazardous substances and their reportable quantities.
notes.back: A: The Environmental Protection Agency's list at title 40, section 302.4
notes.choices:
A) The Environmental Protection Agency's list at title 40, section 302.4
B) Table 1 of appendix A to § 172.101
C) Column 10 of the HMT
D) Appendix B to § 172.101
notes.choicesExplained: B: from 2 December 2026 appendix A refers to the title 40 list instead of listing substances. C: column 10 covers vessel stowage. D: appendix B lists marine pollutants.

notes.front: At what concentrations in a solution or mixture does a listed material count as a marine pollutant?
notes.explanation: Materials flagged as severe in appendix B take the lower threshold.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 171 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 171.8, “Marine pollutant”, p. 30
notes.evidence: Ten percent by weight of the solution or mixture for materials listed in the appendix; or (2) One percent by weight of the solution or mixture for materials that are identified as severe marine pollutants in the appendix.
notes.back: 10 percent by weight or more; 1 percent or more for a severe marine pollutant.

notes.front: A marine pollutant is not named in the HMT and meets no definition in Classes 1 to 8. How must it be offered?
notes.explanation: If it did meet a Class 1 to 8 definition, its class would be set by § 173.2a instead.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (revised as of 1 October 2025), Appendix B to § 172.101, para. 2, p. 195
notes.evidence: If a marine pollutant not listed by name or by synonym in the § 172.101 Table does not meet the definition of any Class 1 through 8, then you must offer it for transportation under the most appropriate of the following two Class 9 entries:
notes.back: Under the most appropriate of two Class 9 entries: environmentally hazardous substances, liquid, n.o.s. (UN 3082) or solid, n.o.s. (UN 3077).

notes.front: A mixture contains 3 percent by weight of a substance flagged in appendix B as a severe marine pollutant. Does the mixture meet the marine pollutant definition for that substance?
notes.explanation: Severe marine pollutants take the 1 percent threshold.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 171 (revised as of 1 October 2025), § 171.8, “Marine pollutant”, p. 30
notes.evidence: One percent by weight of the solution or mixture for materials that are identified as severe marine pollutants in the appendix.
notes.back: D: Yes: severe marine pollutants count at 1 percent or more
notes.choices:
A) No: the threshold is 10 percent
B) No: mixtures are never marine pollutants
C) Only if the substance is also named in the HMT
D) Yes: severe marine pollutants count at 1 percent or more
notes.choicesExplained: A: 10 percent is for listed materials that are not severe marine pollutants. B: the definition expressly covers solutions and mixtures. C: marine pollutants in appendix B are not necessarily named in the HMT.
